extraction.title: Twenty Years of Personality Computing: Threats, Challenges and Future Directions
extraction.venue: ACM Computing Surveys, Vol. 58, No. 11, Article 293 (April 2026). Metadata hint had venue and DOI blank; corrected from the PDF header.
extraction.document_type: Survey / review article (PRISMA 2020-guided literature review, with a state-of-the-art table and an ethics section on LLMs)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 3,221 lines of _text/bac6a6557620.txt, covering front matter, Sections 1 to 4, Tables 1 to 13, Figures 1 to 3, and the full reference list (299 entries). Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied for this task, so paul_markup is empty. The PDF text export itself was not checked for embedded annotations beyond what the text file shows.
extraction.research_question: What has Personality Computing (computational recognition, perception and synthesis of personality) achieved over roughly two decades in methods, applications and benchmarks, what ethical threats does it pose (especially with LLMs), and what future directions should researchers take? (Introduction, p.2-3.)
extraction.theory: Personality psychology trait models: Big Five/OCEAN and FFM as the main model (p.4), with MBTI and DISC judged to lack validity (p.4-5). Trait versus state distinction (p.3). Brunswik lens model of interpersonal perception, with ecological validity, representation validity and perceptual judgment (p.5). Three-task framing of Personality Recognition, Perception and Synthesis (p.5). Three LLM ethics themes: Machine Personality, Personality Hacking, Personality Safety (p.22).
extraction.data: No primary data. The unit of analysis is the published literature. Corpus: 163 records identified, 152 after deduplication, 26 excluded on quality grounds, and 129 papers reported as included (45 text, 15 image, 7 audio, 25 video, 20 hybrid, 7 LLM, 10 LLM-ethics). Note: 152 minus 26 is 126, so the stated category counts (129) do not reconcile with the stated screening arithmetic (p.12). Benchmarks in Table 2 (p.9-10): Essays (about 2,500 persons, text, 2007 era); MyPersonality (about 6,000,000 persons per Table 2 and text p.9, mixed, Facebook, 2007-2015); Big5Mbti (1,800 persons, text, multi-language); PANDORA talks (about 10,000, text); WCPR2013 (250 persons); WCPR2014 (about 460); PAN-AP-2015 (294 X users); PersIA (22 persons, 6,552 items); Personality Simulation 1 (400 entries, tabular). Period covered: from the 1999 Essays/LIWC work to 2025 LLM studies (field start 2005 per p.2).
extraction.method: Narrative/systematic review following PRISMA 2020 (p.12). Search combined modality keywords with personality aliases on the web and in Google Scholar and Scopus. Iterative reference-list expansion to transitive closure. Scopus citation network built in Gephi, with in-degree of 5 or more shown as a foundational-works graph (Fig. 2, p.6-7). Two-phase screening: inclusive first pass, then a pruning pass that excluded inconsistent or flawed work (small samples, weak train/validation/test setup, no comparison to prior methods, unavailable data or code; example Souri et al. [252] excluded, p.12). A single reviewer handled valid articles; at least one more reviewer handled exclusion candidates (p.12). Separate state-of-the-art (SotA) table limited to open-science works, Big Five targets, and F1, accuracy or Rho metrics (Table 3, p.10-11). Section 3 categorizes systems by data modality with Big Five cue tables (Tables 5, 9, 11) and algorithm/feature/data-source matrices (Tables 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12). Section 3.5 surveys 10 LLM-ethics papers (Table 13).
extraction.identification: None. This is a review article with no causal design, instrument or identification strategy of its own.
extraction.scope: Population: human digital footprints (text, images, audio, video, social media metadata, phone and smartphone logs, EEG, physiological data) and LLM outputs. Institutions: academic Personality Computing research plus applied sectors (marketing, recruiting, healthcare, forensics, credit, education). Era: 1999 to 2025 references, field started 2005 (p.2). Language: mostly English, with some Chinese, Indonesian and multilingual work (p.6-7). Domain is personality computing, not legislative, lobbying or election research per se.

key_findings.finding: SotA for Personality Recognition from text is an average correlation of about 0.3 over a baseline of 0.133, from WASSA shared tasks.
key_findings.location: Section 2.6, p.11; Table 3, p.10 (WASSA2024 Rho 0.300; PANDORA talks Rho 0.292)
key_findings.numbers: Rho about 0.30 vs baseline 0.133

key_findings.finding: Early shared tasks (Speaker Trait 2012, WCPR 2013/2014, PAN-AP 2015) reached F1 slightly above 0.7, with accuracy between 0.62 and 0.84 depending on input data. A T5 zero-shot replication on PAN-AP-2015 gave averaged F1 0.711.
key_findings.numbers: F1 about 0.70-0.72; accuracy 0.62-0.84; replication F1 0.711; PAN-AP-2015 accuracy 0.840 in Table 3

key_findings.finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with zero-shot prompting infer Big Five traits from Facebook status updates at an average correlation of 0.29, comparable to specialized ML models (Peters and Matz 2024).
key_findings.location: Section 2.6, p.11; Table 3, p.10; Table 12, p.22
key_findings.numbers: average r = 0.29; WASSA-style Rho scale

key_findings.finding: Personality Synthesis (role-play LLM self-assessment consistency) has SotA averaged accuracy around 0.75. Table 3 lists Klinkert et al. 2024 at 0.740 and Wang et al. 2024 at 0.766.
key_findings.numbers: accuracy about 0.75 (0.740 and 0.766)

key_findings.finding: Computational Personality Perception SotA is a convergent validity of Rho = 0.30 (meta-analysis of computer prediction studies), close to human perception meta-analytic convergent validity of rho = 0.38. Data source (social media, video, smartphone) significantly affects variance explained. Effect sizes are flagged as not fully comparable across settings.
key_findings.location: Section 2.6, p.11 (citing Hinds and Joinson 2024 [119]); Table 3, p.10 (Hinds et al. 2024 marked 0.300 with a comparability caveat)
key_findings.numbers: computer rho = 0.30; human rho = 0.38

key_findings.finding: Among 45 text-based systems, SVMs were the most used algorithm (20 articles), followed by neural networks (12) and Naive Bayes (10). Social network data was the most common source (27 articles), followed by Essays (15). Psycho-linguistic features were the most common homogeneous feature type (16), with broader word-based features in 20 articles.
key_findings.numbers: SVM 20; NN 12; NB 10; social network 27; Essays 15; psycho-linguistic 16; broader 20

key_findings.finding: Among 20 hybrid systems, SVMs (8), linear regression (6) and decision trees (5) were most used. Social media metadata (12) and smartphone usage or call data (6) were the most common sources. Example: Golbeck et al. 2011 combined Facebook friend networks with LIWC features.
key_findings.location: Section 3.3, p.19; Table 10, p.19; Table 11, p.21
key_findings.numbers: SVM 8; linear regression 6; decision tree 5; social metadata 12; smartphone 6

key_findings.finding: Image-based systems (15 studies, 2014-2021) rely mainly on social media images, with NN and SVM most common and CNN use rising. Openness links to artistic images; Conscientiousness to conventional, detailed images; Extraversion to number of people in images.

Video-based systems (25 studies, 2008-2022) show that audio-visual cues carry trait information. Biel et al. 2012 found Extraversion and Emotional Stability carried the largest and smallest sets of informative cues, respectively.
key_findings.numbers: 25 studies

key_findings.finding: MBTI and DISC have well-documented validity problems and should not be used in scientific work or as ground truth, although MBTI labels are easier to classify than Big Five scores.
key_findings.location: Section 2.2, p.4-5; Section 2.6 p.20; Section 4 p.25
key_findings.numbers: n/a

key_findings.finding: LLM-based systems (7 articles) have shifted Personality Recognition toward zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and Personality Synthesis toward role-play prompting. Trend toward MBTI prediction. Gan et al. 2022 report significant (p<0.01) MBTI perception on 41,800 faces, but most effect sizes are small (below 0.2 Cohen's h).
key_findings.numbers: 7 articles; 41,800 facial images; Cohen's h below 0.2

key_findings.finding: LLMs show consistent trait-like profiles (high Agreeableness, high Openness, low Neuroticism). Induced personality can shift safety, jailbreak resistance and fairness. Conscientiousness is associated with safer outputs. The paper argues LLM personality should be treated as a core safety concern.
key_findings.numbers: 10 LLM-ethics articles

key_findings.finding: Threat analysis: personality-aware marketing was used to influence voting in several elections; personality-aware systems can reach deep intimacy with users; personality-aware credit scoring risks social marginalization; personality-aware friend recommendation may strengthen echo chambers.
key_findings.location: Section 4.2, p.24-25 (cites [79] for voting, [143] for intimacy, [262] for echo chambers, [291] for credit)
key_findings.numbers: n/a

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: standardize on correlation coefficients (Rho) for all tasks; discourage median splits; host benchmarks on GitHub, Kaggle or Hugging Face; use Personality Synthesis to create synthetic anonymous data; use Personality Recognition to alter digital footprints and mask cues; add explainable AI to Perception; collaborate with cybersecurity, computational social science and computational history communities.
key_findings.numbers: n/a

limitations: No dedicated limitations section. Limitations stated inline: Hinds and Joinson effect sizes must be read with caution because human and computer settings differ in methods and data (p.11).
The SotA tables include only open-science works that target Big Five with F1, accuracy or Rho, so the table is a selected set, not a full census (p.10-11).

Inclusion relied on a single reviewer for most articles, with extra reviewers only for exclusion candidates (p.12). Reported screening counts do not reconcile: 152 minus 26 is 126, not the 129 reported as included (p.12).

Table 3 mixes metrics across studies (F1, accuracy and Rho) and marks some values as non-comparable (p.10). Several tables rely on author-assigned categories (for example Table 4 algorithm grouping, p.12).
Many cited works are small-sample (for example PersIA 22 persons, WCPR2013 250 persons), and the review itself notes that small samples and weak validation were grounds for exclusion (p.12).
Authors disclaim the causal and validity status of MBTI-based results and note LLM personality may not be a true psychological state (p.4-5, p.22).
Scope is computer-science oriented. Authors state the review targets a computer science readership (p.3).

summary_md:
Celli and colleagues review about twenty years of Personality Computing. They follow PRISMA 2020 and report 129 included papers, although the screening arithmetic in the paper gives 126. The review covers three tasks: Recognition (self-reported traits), Perception (traits as observers judge them) and Synthesis (traits that machines generate). Across text, image, audio, video, hybrid and LLM systems, the reported state of the art is modest. Text recognition reaches an average correlation of about 0.30 against a 0.133 baseline. Zero-shot GPT models reach r = 0.29 on Facebook posts, about the same as specialized models. Computer perception has a convergent validity of 0.30, against 0.38 for human judges, and the authors warn that these settings are not fully comparable. Most text systems are SVMs on psycholinguistic features (LIWC/MRC), drawn from Essays and social-network data. Biel et al. found that Extraversion carries the most audio-visual cues and Emotional Stability the fewest. The review recommends reporting rank correlations rather than median splits, judges MBTI and DISC invalid, and calls LLM personality a safety problem. It also lists personality-aware persuasion in elections as a threat.

For Melange, the paper sets an outside ceiling on what text- and audio-derived traits can deliver. It also places the system's validation targets on Brunswik's lens model. The RKH comparison is Recognition against a target that uses the same method as the system. The Personality on the Hill panels are Perception. Neither is a self-report criterion, so the system's figures do not line up with the paper's state-of-the-art rows. The paper also explains why the system was right to move receptivity off lexical traits and onto behavior. The cue pattern by modality suggests that audio work should start with Extraversion, not Neuroticism. Every cross-study comparison below is UNVERIFIED (DE-062); no second path has reproduced it.

bearings.paper_claim: Text Personality Recognition state of the art is an average correlation of about 0.30 (WASSA2024 Rho 0.300; PANDORA 0.292) over a 0.133 baseline, measured against self-report inventories. Among 45 text systems, SVMs (20) on psycholinguistic or LIWC-family features (16 homogeneous, 20 broader) dominate, and Essays plus social-network data are the main sources.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2.6, p.11; Table 3, p.10; Section 3.1 and Table 4, p.12-13
bearings.system_side: Closed-vocabulary rates (LIWC-analog, Empath, MATTR, concreteness) are z-scored within the corpus and combined with Mairesse SMOreg or published-correlate weights, then refit to RKH targets. Held-out CV against RKH averages .350 (E .510 down to O .214). This is the Mairesse/LIWC lineage the survey treats as the field's historical core.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 0.30 ceiling is measured against self-report on general users (Facebook, Essays, Reddit). The system's .350 is measured against RKH, which is itself a Mairesse-LIWC text estimate of the same legislators, so the two figures share a method and are not comparable. The .350 must not be read as above the field ceiling. Against an independent self-report or observer criterion, expect values at or below about 0.30. Elite speech is staff-written and genre-shifted, which probably lowers the figure further.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)|Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Brunswik lens framing separates Recognition (self-report target) from Perception (observer-attributed traits). Computer Perception convergent validity is rho = 0.30, against rho = 0.38 for human perception (Hinds & Joinson 2024 meta-analysis), with a caveat that the settings are not comparable. The paper recommends standardizing on rank correlation and discouraging median splits.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2.3 (Brunswik lens), p.5; Section 2.6, p.11; Table 3, p.10; Section 4.2 recommendations, p.25
bearings.system_side: Text traits are validated separately against the Personality on the Hill Senate insider and academic panels, as per-panel correlations, not dichotomized. E and A pass both panels; O, C and N pass one panel each.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Expert and insider panels are observer judgments, so the right benchmark is the Perception figure (0.30 machine, 0.38 human), not the Recognition rows. The survey's figures come from mixed populations (social media, video, smartphone), not U.S. senators, whose public personas are managed. The system's continuous per-panel correlations already follow the paper's Rho-not-median-split advice.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria|Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria]]

bearings.paper_claim: Zero-shot GPT-3.5/4 infers Big Five from Facebook status updates at an average r = 0.29, comparable to specialized ML (Peters & Matz 2024). That is parity, not superiority. LLMs also show stable machine-personality profiles (high Agreeableness, high Openness, low Neuroticism) that are separate from the person being rated.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2.6, p.11; Table 12, p.22; Section 3.5 and Table 13, p.22-23
bearings.system_side: The Pink LLM reader de-identifies names, state, party and title before item-level scoring, codes 'cannot tell' as 0, and is display-only. The Pink x behavioral diagonal is +0.064, below the 0.12 bar (fail). CT-CM models an LLM method factor.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's parity result uses users' own casual posts scored against self-report. The system scores de-identified, staff-shaped political text against behavioral criteria, so a lower figure is expected. A built-in LLM trait profile is one plausible source of the single method or halo factor that CT-CM targets, but the survey does not test that mechanism. The evidence does not show that LLM readers should beat lexical ones.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model|LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model]]

bearings.paper_claim: Across 25 video and audio-visual systems (2008-2022), nonverbal cues carry trait information. Biel et al. 2012 found that Extraversion has the largest set of informative cues and Emotional Stability the smallest. OpenSMILE features are a standard audio input.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.3, p.17-18; Tables 8-9; Table 2, p.9
bearings.system_side: The system extracts 88 eGeMAPSv02 functionals per clip with openSMILE, mean-pooled per member. The audio-prosody N pilot MISSed at N=90. Audio is display-only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Biel's cue counts come from vlog video, not congressional hearings, and its targets are observer impressions. If those counts carry over, an audio channel would be most likely to work for Extraversion, and the N (Emotional Stability) target that MISSed was the least promising choice. Any new audio look still needs its own preregistration. The paper gives no estimate for edited broadcast audio such as NPR, where venue confounds are large.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: Machine trait estimates converge at about 0.30 with criteria, so a noisy recognized trait carries roughly 9% shared variance. Separately, the paper names personality-aware marketing used to influence voting as a threat and calls for explainability in Perception systems.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2.6, p.11; Section 4.2, p.24-25 (cites [79], [243])
bearings.system_side: The default receptivity basis is behavioral: susc = .40 coop + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance, blended with the persona channel at PERSONA_W 0.30. The lexical susceptibility composite (.40A + .30N - .20C - .10E) is retained only as the RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical revert, after the prereg indicted lexical Big5 for behavioral prediction. Receptivity changes engine multipliers, not rank.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The survey's ceiling supports the system's own finding that lexical traits are too weak to drive behavior-facing multipliers. It says nothing about behavioral dispositions such as cooperation_v2, whose validity rests on the project's own records. The ethics threat is about voters and consumers, not legislators, so it is context for how outputs are worded, not evidence against the layer. Per owner ruling, PERSONA_W stays as it is.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)|Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)]]

gaps_exposed: No self-report criterion exists for any member, so the system cannot place its trait scores on the paper's Recognition scale. RKH convergence (.350) uses the same method and is not a Recognition benchmark.
Validation records do not state which Brunswik task (Recognition or Perception) each look tests, so field benchmarks get mixed up in summaries.
There is no audio or video Extraversion look, even though the survey reports Extraversion as the trait with the most nonverbal cues. Audio effort went to N, the trait with the fewest.
There is no written ethics or misuse note for a personality-aware persuasion layer. The paper names personality-targeted persuasion in elections as a primary threat and asks for explainability.
flags: The paper's own screening counts do not reconcile: 152 after deduplication minus 26 excluded is 126, but 129 are reported as included (p.12). Quote its corpus totals with that caveat.

Do not quote the system's lexical CV .350 against RKH as matching or exceeding the field's 0.30 state of the art. The criteria differ (a method-shared text estimate versus self-report), and the paper itself flags cross-setting effect sizes as not comparable.

Personality-aware persuasion appears in the paper's threat list (Section 4.2). The receptivity layer is that class of system, aimed at legislators. Wording should describe its traits as heuristic model inputs, not as measured psychology, and every figure needs its window and denominator.
This paper argues for neither of the rejected SNA proposals (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, or per-edge volume normalization). There is no conflict with D-021 or D-025.
All cross-study comparisons here are agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul in part. He calls Ramey 'dated but foundational', and Celli confirms that the SVM-on-LIWC lineage was the field's core for most of two decades. Paul endorses LLM trait reading on the strength of Birkenmaier. Celli's evidence (Peters & Matz, r = 0.29) shows LLMs at parity with specialized models, not ahead of them, and the system's own Pink reader failed its behavioral bar (+0.064 against 0.12). Paul's notes on receptivity, which want psychological traits as edge parameters, are stale relative to the system. Lexical Big5 was indicted for behavioral prediction and the default basis is now behavioral. The survey's modest ceilings support that move more than Paul's annotations do. He has no annotation on this paper.

related.why: Ramey applies the Mairesse/LIWC Recognition pipeline that Celli reviews as the field's text core to legislators. big5_traits.py copies it.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations. It gives the feature-level effect sizes behind Celli's text state of the art of about 0.30.
A meta-analysis of predicting traits from digital footprints. It covers the same Recognition evidence on social media that Celli summarizes.
Provides the Senate expert and insider panels. In Celli's lens framing these are Perception criteria, and the system validates against them.
An elite-specific validation of LLM trait reading. Celli's Peters & Matz parity result frames how far LLM gains can be expected to go.
A parallel 2025 survey of ML and deep-learning personality detection covering the same algorithm and dataset landscape.
An earlier paper by the same first author on Emotional Stability cues in Twitter conversations. It is part of the WCPR-era work the survey reviews.
An audio and multimodal self-reported personality recognition benchmark, relevant to the survey's audio and video findings and to the system's prosody MISS.
Quantifies the returns to political microtargeting, the persuasion threat Celli names in Section 4.2.
An LLM-generated personality-targeted political persuasion study. It is an empirical instance of the Machine Personality and personality-hacking concerns Celli raises.
The Pennebaker LIWC and Essays lineage (Pennebaker & King 1999) is the survey's founding benchmark and the basis of the system's affective-N and lexical features.

backlinks.why: A review of threats in personality computing. Rubio's selection-leakage ambiguity and failed replication are examples of the reproducibility problems it covers.

meta.title: RELINK: Edge Activation for Closed Network Influence Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning

extraction.title: RELINK: Edge Activation for Closed Network Influence Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (full text, 8 pages of body plus references, 12-page ACM format per the reference block)
extraction.coverage: Read the whole extracted text file (2,054 lines, 77,630 chars) in two chunks: lines 1-1224 and 1225-2054. Covers front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries, embedding (Sec. 4), MDP and DDQN training (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6, Tables/Figures 1-6), conclusion, GenAI disclosure and the full reference list. No Paul markup was supplied for this PDF (none), so paul_markup is empty. The paper contains no lobbying, election, persuasion/turnout, legislator or text-measurement content; those topics are absent, not just unaddressed in the excerpt.
extraction.research_question: How can we learn effective edge activation strategies for influence maximization in closed (privacy-constrained) social networks, where node-level activation is infeasible and propagation is limited to a budgeted subset of existing edges? (Abstract; Sec. 1)
extraction.theory: No social theory is developed. The diffusion basis is the Independent Cascade (IC) model (Kempe et al. 2003, ref. [49]), with the IM-CSN formulation of Huang et al. (2022, ref. [46]) as the problem definition. Motivation is privacy-focused and invitation-only platforms (Signal, Discord, Instagram Close Friends, Slack, Nextdoor), Sec. 1. The learning side is an MDP with n-step Double DQN (van Hasselt et al. 2016, ref. [85]).
extraction.data: Training: 40 synthetic graphs (10 each from Barabasi-Albert, Watts-Strogatz, stochastic block model, Erdos-Renyi), node counts 25-150 (Sec. 6.1). Testing: 20 real-world social networks, unit = network (Table 1), with sizes from Residence hall (217 nodes, 2,674 edges) to Slashdot Feb'09 (82,140 nodes, 549,202 edges). Undirected edges are converted to directed pairs (Huang et al. preprocessing). Seed sets: sampled from top 5% by degree, |S| in {5, 50, 100, 200}; budget k in {5, 10, 20}. The text reports 480 experimental configurations over the 20 networks (Sec. 6.1, 6.2). Time period of the real data is not stated. Weighting: random IC probabilities in [0,1] and uniform 0.5 (Sec. 6.1).
extraction.method: Edge-level DRL for IM-CSN. (1) Influence-aware node embeddings combining five feature classes: Louvain community ID and size, approximate betweenness, degree, bridge score, clustering coefficient; path features (2-hop neighbour count, path diversity, RMPP-inspired most-probable-path feature from Chaoji et al. 2012); outgoing-edge weight mean/max/variance; seed indicators and seed distance; Node2Vec embedding; SVD reduction to d=16 (Sec. 4.1). (2) Edge-aware aggregation with learned relevance score alpha_ij = sigma(a^T[h_i||h_j] * w_ij), two-hop aggregation via A^2, gated update and degree-normalized residual (Sec. 4.2). (3) MDP: state = partial subgraph, action = activate an edge respecting the per-node out-degree budget k, reward = exact marginal influence gain under IC (Sec. 5.1). (4) Edge Q-values from projected node features, edge weight, and a penalty on accumulated incoming weight (Sec. 5.2). (5) Training by n-step Double DQN with EMA target network, replay buffer of 1M transitions, epsilon-greedy exploration, valid-action restriction; true marginal gains are computed only at training time (Sec. 5.3). (6) Inference: greedy argmax over action-masked Q-values, one edge per step, until no valid actions remain; max steps O(|V|k) (Sec. 5.4). Hardware: NVIDIA A40 GPU, Xeon Silver 4314 CPU; PyTorch, Adam (Sec. 6.1). Baselines: Degree, FoF, Random (five-run average), PSNA (Huang et al. 2022) (Sec. 6.1).

short_quotes.quote: the first DRL framework for edge-level influence maximization in privacy-constrained networks

summary_md:
RELINK (Arya, Ghosh, Maruyama and Srinivasan, CIKM 2025) treats influence maximization in "closed" networks as an edge-selection problem. The seed set is fixed, and each node may switch on at most k of its outgoing edges. Spread can travel only along the edges that were switched on. The method builds influence-aware node embeddings and trains an edge-scoring Double DQN on 40 small synthetic graphs (25-150 nodes). The same trained policy then runs on 20 public real networks. Spread is simulated under Independent Cascade (IC) with random or uniform 0.5 edge weights, using 100,000 Monte Carlo draws repeated 10 times. RELINK beats Random, Degree and FoF in about 462-464 of 480 configurations, and beats the IM-CSN baseline PSNA in 456 of 480. The margin is widest at small edge budgets and narrows as k grows. On dense graphs PSNA can win at small seed sets. RELINK is slower than PSNA on small and medium graphs and only catches up on large ones. The paper offers no optimality guarantee and says the objective is non-submodular. No legislative, lobbying or empirical-persuasion data are involved.

The paper matters here because Melange already names RELINK as the design source for its cosponsor recruitment routes. These are `cosponsor_route.py` (champion seeds, at most K=5 asks per recruiter) and the dashboard's closed-network Max-cascade route (`closedCascadeRoute`, 6 edges, fan-out 2). What the system took is the problem framing: an action is an edge, and each node has an out-degree budget. It did not take the learned policy or any of RELINK's evidence. Both builds are hand-tuned greedy heuristics. They are close relatives of the baselines RELINK outperforms, applied to a dense 533-node graph that sits in the regime where RELINK's edge is smallest. The paper therefore supports the code's own disclaimer that no (1-1/e) guarantee applies. It gives no empirical support for K, the fan-out or the kernel probabilities. It also weakens the case for replacing the money optimizer with a learned policy, because that optimizer's greedy is already exact for its separable concave objective. Everything in this mapping is agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: IM-CSN as edge activation: seeds are fixed, each node may activate at most k of its out-edges (k in {5,10,20}), and the reward is the marginal IC spread. A DRL edge policy beats Random, Degree and FoF in 462-464 of 480 configurations and PSNA in 456 of 480. Gains reach about 15%, mainly at small k.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3 and 5.1 (MDP, per-node out-degree budget); Sec. 6.2-6.3, Figures 3 and 6
bearings.system_side: The docstring credits 'RELINK + MOPBD*'. Champion seeds each whip at most K=5 colleagues (out-degree budget). The recruiter list is built greedily, ranked by a value-per-dollar score (gain - lambda(1-p))/cost for lambda in {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, and a Pareto front is taken. The optional MC reach runs IC over the induced node subgraph of seeds plus recruits. That is all edges among those nodes, not only the activated edges as IM-CSN requires. K=5 and CEDGE are unestimated dials.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the problem formulation transfers: edge actions under a per-node budget. The performance evidence does not. RELINK's wins are for a trained DDQN policy, and this component is a greedy heuristic. The spread being maximized is simulated IC on public online graphs with random or uniform 0.5 weights. Melange's kernel probabilities (x/(x+6), with an unestimated saturation constant) are mostly lower, a regime the paper never tested. The paper also has no evidence that a per-legislator 'whip capacity' K exists or is near 5. Treat the whip capacity as a modeling prior.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Cosponsor recruitment route finder (Pareto front)|Cosponsor recruitment route finder (Pareto front)]]

bearings.paper_claim: The IM-CSN objective is non-submodular, so greedy marginal-gain edge selection carries no approximation guarantee. Among heuristics, Degree ranks last with FoF next to it under k=20 uniform weights, and Random and PSNA do best. On dense graphs (email-Eu-core, wiki-Vote, sx-mathoverflow) RELINK's advantage over PSNA reverses at small seed sets.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.1 (non-submodular objective); Sec. 6.2 Figure 4 (k=20 baseline ordering); Sec. 6.3 Figure 6 (dense-graph cases)
bearings.system_side: The dashboard Max-cascade route grows a closed-network edge tree from the selected member: 6 edges, at most 2 asks per recruiter. Each edge is scored as arrival x marginal x (0.75 + 0.25 PR/PRMAX), and the code says it makes no (1-1/e) claim. budgetRecruit is a node-seed max-coverage greedy that does claim (1-1/e) on its submodular coverage proxy. A test pins the hub-convergence disclosure ruling.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Two parts carry over: the non-submodularity point, and the warning that degree- or hub-favouring heuristics are weak under per-node edge budgets. Both are structural and support the code's existing disclaimer. The (1-1/e) claim on budgetRecruit holds only for its node-coverage proxy, not for an edge-activation spread. The paper does not show whether hub convergence in a 533-node House cosponsor graph is good or bad, because dense small graphs are where its comparisons were least favourable to RELINK. Treat the route outputs as heuristic model outputs, never as introduction or access probabilities.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Best-sponsor, multi-target tree and budget max-coverage modes|Best-sponsor, multi-target tree and budget max-coverage modes]]

bearings.paper_claim: The learned edge policy is slower than PSNA on small and medium graphs. It becomes competitive or faster only as graphs grow to tens of thousands of nodes. Training cost 6,257 s because exact marginal gains are computed. The gains come in a non-submodular combinatorial setting.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 6.2 Q3 (Figure 5, runtime); Sec. 6.4 (training cost); Sec. 5.1
bearings.system_side: CELF lazy greedy over per-member concave dollar chunks. The docstring states that in a fixed stance state the objective is separable and concave, so greedy is the exact discrete optimum. A Golovin-Krause bound is kept as a diagnostic. The dashboard's budgetRecruit comment already says 'no ML needed at our scale'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: RELINK's case for a learned policy rests on scale and on non-submodular edge choice. Neither applies to a 533-member, separable, concave money allocation, where greedy is already exact. A learned policy could matter only for the conversion-replanning path, which is not certified, or for a future edge-level recruitment optimizer. Even then the paper's evidence comes from synthetic IC benchmarks, not legislative outcomes.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Joint CU budget optimizer|Joint CU budget optimizer]]

bearings.paper_claim: Spread is estimated with 100,000 Monte Carlo IC simulations, repeated 10 times, to separate methods whose spread ratios fall roughly between 0.85 and 1.15.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 6.1 (evaluation protocol); Figure 6 colour scale
bearings.system_side: Competitive IC uses keyed splitmix64 common random numbers, with MC=20 for the frontier and MC=40 for the scenario and route runs. The splitmix64 draw function is sm64, and the shared kernel is build_P.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a benchmark for how many simulations are needed to resolve differences of 5-15% between alternatives. CRN reduces variance in paired comparisons, so far fewer draws may be enough for rank decisions. Comparing absolute spreads across routes or Pareto points at MC 20-40 is not supported by this paper. The adequacy of MC=20-40 is still the system's own claim (mc_stability_check), and this paper does not test it.

gaps_exposed: No learned or optimized edge-activation policy exists. Both RELINK-labelled builds (cosponsor_route.py and closedCascadeRoute) are greedy heuristics like the baselines RELINK beats. Neither has been compared against even a Random edge baseline, which ranked among the strongest heuristics in RELINK's Figure 4.

cosponsor_route.py mc_spread lets activation run over every edge among the selected nodes, not only the activated edges. That is not the IM-CSN closed-network semantics the docstring claims. The dashboard Max route's cascadeReach then runs an open-network cascade from the recruited set.

The per-recruiter budgets (K=5 in cosponsor_route, fanout=2 and edgeBudget=6 in the dashboard) are not estimated from any observed whip or ask behaviour, and the paper gives no basis for legislative values.
There is no sensitivity check of route rankings to the budget k. RELINK shows method ordering changes with k (its gap to PSNA narrows as k grows).
The paper's evidence is IC-only, with random or uniform 0.5 weights. The system's low-probability kernel regime (crypto p_max 0.23, CU 0.52) is untested territory for any edge-activation claim.
flags: Labelling caution: the code and brain call these routes the 'RELINK design' and 'RELINK Pareto' (cosponsor_route.py:3; make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:675,828; brain topic 2026-06-feature-melange-scenario-model-build). The system borrows only the problem framing. No RELINK performance result transfers to these heuristics, so any claim citing RELINK's '15%' or '456/480' for Melange routes would be a misattribution.

Route outputs (expected recruits, 'all asks hold' percentages, Pareto spread) are heuristic model outputs under unestimated ASKM, K and kernel constants. Under D-025 they must not be presented as introduction, access or closeness probabilities.

The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization), so there is nothing to flag there. It uses no LDA data, so D-021 does not apply.
This whole mapping is agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces it.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. His nearest positions concern the joint optimizer, the budget frontier and the cosponsor route. For the optimizer he expects a learned policy (GCOMB) to replace greedy at scale. RELINK is a learned edge policy, but it pays off on runtime only for graphs much larger than the 533-member House. Its spread advantage comes in a non-submodular setting. The joint optimizer's separable concave money problem is neither, so greedy is already exact there. On that component Paul's expectation runs ahead of what this evidence supports, and the system's own 'no ML needed at our scale' comment matches the paper better. On the cosponsor route, Paul said D* Lite and LPA* replanning should be the operational layer. RELINK is silent on incremental replanning, so that gap remains. RELINK did supply the per-recruiter budget idea that was built. The brain records RELINK in the June 2026 research corpus as 'maps to co-sponsor campaigns'. That note is not wrong but is incomplete: it does not say that the built version is a greedy heuristic rather than RELINK's DRL, or that RELINK's evidence covers synthetic IC spread on public online graphs, not legislators.

related.why: cosponsor_route.py cites RELINK and MOPBD* together. RELINK supplies the edge-budget formulation and MOPBD* the multi-objective Pareto routing concept.
Same family of reinforcement learning for influence maximization. Chen's contingency-aware seeding is implemented as the seed gate, while RELINK's edge policy is borrowed only as a formulation.
Another DRL influence-maximization policy, for complex contagion, the alternative to RELINK's IC-only setting that Paul raises for coalition formation.
Learned influence-maximization policies under limited network access. It is the node-and-sampling analogue of RELINK's constraint of propagating only along chosen edges.
Graph-embedding and GNN influence maximization. RELINK's node2vec, SVD and edge-aware aggregation embedding sits in the same lineage.
Golovin-Krause guarantees need (adaptive) submodularity. RELINK states that IM-CSN is non-submodular and claims no guarantee, so those bounds do not extend to edge-activation routes.

Likely the 2026 Scientific Reports benchmark the dashboard cites for using a PageRank prior in route scoring. Its heuristic-versus-greedy findings sit beside RELINK's learned-versus-heuristic results.
Both build on Kempe-style IC cascades. Bharathi's competitive IC is the system's coalition cascade, while RELINK's edge activation assumes a single cascade.
Both evaluate influence maximization under the Independent Cascade model, using Monte Carlo spread estimates as the outcome.

backlinks.why: The dashboard's closedCascadeRoute cites RELINK and correctly disclaims (1-1/e) for non-submodular IM-CSN, consistent with Thm 9.

meta.title: Partisan Cue Receptivity: Bounded Rationality vs Expressive Utility
meta.venue: The Journal of Politics, vol. 82, no. 3 (July 2020), pp. 1061-1077. Published online May 11, 2020.

extraction.title: Partisan Cue Receptivity: Bounded Rationality vs Expressive Utility
extraction.venue: The Journal of Politics, vol. 82, no. 3 (July 2020), pp. 1061-1077. Published online May 11, 2020.
extraction.document_type: Journal article: survey experiments (five primary, two ancillary) with an individual-data meta-analysis; studies 3 and 4 were preregistered replications.
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 2,104 lines of _text\d919f3743193.txt (main text pp. 1061-1076, tables, figure notes, footnotes, discussion and references). Appendices A-I are cited but are not in the file, so appendix-only results are reported only as the main text describes them. Metadata hint corrected: full author names and journal details added from the text; the hint's author list and blank venue/DOI fields were incomplete. Annotations: one JSON file with 24 items, all of type Highlight (22 yellow, 2 green); no sticky notes or typed comments exist, so every note field is empty.
extraction.research_question: Why do citizens follow partisan cues when forming policy judgments? Is cue receptivity strongest among people with low cognitive resources (bounded rationality, cue-taking as effort-saving), or among people with both strong partisan social identity and high cognitive resources (expressive utility, effortful identity-protective reasoning)?
extraction.theory: Bounded rationality (Simon 1972; Kam 2005; Lupia and McCubbins 1998): cues are heuristics that let low-resource citizens adopt value-consistent positions without costly effort, so cue receptivity should be highest among those low in cognitive resources. Expressive utility (Kahan 2013; Petersen et al. 2013; Lodge and Taber 2013; Groenendyk 2013): cue-following is identity-protective motivated reasoning, so the strongest cue receptivity should appear among people with strong partisan social identity who also have the resources to rationalize the party position. The authors treat the strong-identity-by-high-resource interaction as the key distinctive prediction of expressive utility (p. 1063).
extraction.data: Study 1 (food irradiation): Survey Sampling International panel, July 2016; 883 respondents, 747 analyzed (136 excluded for no party ID or leaning). Study 2 (farm subsidy): Qualtrics panel, June 2017; 1,302 partisans in text (647 Democrats, 655 Republicans), but Table 3 reports N = 1,258; discrepancy not explained in main text. Study 3 (replication of studies 1 and 2): Bovitz Forthright sample, October 2018, N = 1,911 (appendix C). Study 4 (replication of food irradiation): Amazon MTurk, October 2018, N = 2,509 (appendix D). Individual-data meta-analysis of studies 1-4 (Table 4): 8,116 observations in CRT models, 5,607 in NfC and latent-resource models. Ancillary: US trade policy experiment (July 2016) and Danish ideology experiment (August 2017), both without a no-cues control (appendices H and I). Unit: individual respondent who identifies with or leans toward a party (the Danish study uses ideological identity). Outcome: policy support on a 0-1 scale (study 2 uses a seven-point item rescaled 0-1). Fieldwork 2016-2018.
extraction.method: OLS regression of policy support on in-party and out-party cue dummies (control is omitted category), partisan social identity strength (PSID), one cognitive resource measure, and covariates (gender, age, education, race, party). The bounded rationality test uses cue-by-resource and cue-by-PSID two-way interactions. The expressive utility test uses cue x PSID x resource three-way interactions, plotted as marginal effects at -1 SD, mean, and +1 SD of PSID and resources. Individual-data meta-analysis (studies 1-4, and separately seven experiments for the in-party vs out-party contrast) uses mixed-effects regression with dummies for studies and random intercepts for study and individual. Studies 3 and 4 also measured depth of processing (reading time, thought-listing word count, factual quiz) to test the proposed mechanism.
extraction.identification: Random assignment to cue condition (in-party cue, out-party cue, or control; ancillary studies compare in-party vs out-party only) identifies the cue main effects. Cognitive resources and PSID are pretreatment measures, not manipulated, so the moderation tests are observational interactions. The authors state they cannot identify causal effects of cognitive resources on cue-following (p. 1075). The key tests are three-way interactions, which are individually often nonsignificant. Analyses are OLS with covariates; replication files also run models without covariates (fn. 9).
extraction.scope: US partisans (identifying with or leaning toward a major party) in four online panels (SSI, Qualtrics, Bovitz Forthright, MTurk) fielded 2016-2018. Issues were chosen to be not yet strongly partisan (food irradiation ban; farm subsidies), so findings are about cue-following on newly politicized issues (pp. 1073-1074). Panels are non-probability and the paper does not report their representativeness in the main text. Ancillary Denmark study covers ideology rather than party. Institutional scope: one-shot embedded survey experiments, not repeated elite messaging or real information environments (p. 1076).

key_findings.finding: No support for the bounded rationality prediction. Cue effects are not stronger among low cognitive resource respondents, and in several cases the interaction points the opposite way.
key_findings.location: Abstract p. 1061; study 1 p. 1065; study 2 p. 1066; meta-analysis p. 1070
key_findings.numbers: Study 1: none of six cue x resource interactions significant; in 5 of 6 the sign is opposite to the BR prediction. Study 2: all eight cue x resource interactions opposite to BR; seven nonsignificant, one significant (political knowledge x out-party cue).

key_findings.finding: Study 1 main effects: out-party cue reduces support; in-party cue effect not significant.
key_findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.06 points on 0-1 scale (p < .01); in-party cue +0.03 (not significant). N = 747.

key_findings.finding: Study 1, expressive utility (NfC): among high need-for-cognition respondents, the in-party cue effect grows with partisan identity strength; the three-way term is significant for in-party cue only. CRT and latent-resource three-way terms are not significant.
key_findings.location: Study 1, p. 1065-1066; Table 2 model 4; Figure 1 middle row
key_findings.numbers: In-party x NfC x PSID b = 1.08 (SE .49, p = .027). Simple slope of in-party cue on PSID among high NfC b = .26 (SE .11, p = .019). Out-party analogue b = -.14 (SE .11), not significant. Out-party three-way b = -.53 (SE .51).

key_findings.finding: Study 2, expressive utility: out-party cue effect is larger for strongly identified partisans among high-CRT respondents; political knowledge gives a similar out-party pattern; NfC and latent-resource terms point the expected way but are not significant.
key_findings.numbers: CRT: out-party x PSID x CRT b = -.78 (SE .34, p = .02); in-party three-way b = .29 (SE .37), not significant. Among high-CRT respondents, strong identifiers were more influenced by out-party cues than weak identifiers, b = -.27 (SE .12, p = .02); no parallel for in-party cue. Political knowledge: out-party three-way b = -.68 (SE .28, p = .02); in-party b = .54 (SE .28, p = .05, nearly significant).

key_findings.finding: Study 2 main effects: out-party cue reduces support; in-party cue has no effect.
key_findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.07 on 0-1 scale; in-party cue no significant influence. N = 1,302 in text (Table 3 note reports N = 1,258).

key_findings.finding: Replications (study 3, Bovitz Forthright, and study 4, MTurk) do not support the expressive utility or bounded rationality model in the same way as studies 1 and 2. Study 3 shows again no BR support and mixed EU support; study 4 shows no support for either model.
key_findings.location: Pp. 1069; appendices C.1-C.2 (study 3) and D.1-D.5 (study 4); discussion pp. 1073-1074; fn. 18 p. 1076
key_findings.numbers: Study 3 N = 1,911; study 4 N = 2,509 (Table 1). Study 4 showed no trace of the patterns in other studies; its CRT means were significantly higher than study 3 (app. D.5).

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanism not supported: strongly identified, high-resource partisans did not process policy information more deeply on reading time, thought listing, or factual quiz measures.
key_findings.location: Pp. 1069-1070 (preregistered prediction); appendices C.3-C.5 (study 3) and D.3 (study 4); discussion pp. 1073-1074
key_findings.numbers: Null results across all depth-of-processing measures in studies 3 and 4 (the paper reports no coefficients in the main text). Exploratory reading-time ranking (after Petersen et al. 2013) also found no evidence (fn. 11).

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis of studies 1-4: out-party cue lowers support, in-party cue raises it, and cue effects are not larger among low-resource respondents. Three-way terms are in the expressive utility direction, but only two reach significance.
key_findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.07 points; in-party cue +0.03 points (app. E.2). In-party x PSID x NfC b = .45 (SE .17); in-party x PSID x latent resources b = .50 (SE .20); in-party x PSID x CRT b = .09 (SE .10), not significant. Out-party three-way terms negative but not significant (CRT -.11, NfC -.10, latent -.17).

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis slopes among high-resource respondents: the in-party cue effect increases with partisan identity strength. Substantively, for latent resources the effect rises about 15 percentage points from lowest to highest PSID among high-resource respondents.
key_findings.numbers: Among high resources, in-party cue x PSID slope: CRT b = .09 (SE .04, p < .05); NfC b = .15 (SE .05, p < .01); latent b = .15 (SE .05, p < .01). Out-party x PSID slope among high CRT b = -.09 (SE .05, p < .05).

key_findings.finding: Ancillary in-versus-out-party meta-analysis (seven experiments, including trade policy and Danish ideology): no evidence cue receptivity is stronger among low-resource people; the in-party vs out-party x resource x PSID interactions are all positive; NfC and latent-resource terms are significant, CRT is not.

limitations: Experimental stimuli cover only a small fraction of political messages; variation in issue type, framing and wording may change both the extent and motives of cue-following (p. 1074). Salient, politicized issues may mute effects (p. 1074).

Results depend on the cognitive resource measure: NfC and latent resources support EU more than the CRT, and CRT was consistent with the BR-null finding as well (p. 1075; fn. 8 on 3-item vs 7-item CRT in study 2).
Cognitive resources were not manipulated, so no causal claim about their effect on cue-following. Resources may proxy careful reading or another motivation to toe the party line (p. 1075).
Depth-of-processing mechanism was not supported; the measures (reading time, thought listing, quiz) may not capture rationalization effort (p. 1074). Authors say the mechanism remains untested.
Individual three-way interactions usually did not reach conventional significance; only two of six meta-analytic three-way effects were significant (p. 1075).
Study 4 (MTurk) produced no patterns; the authors suggest platform effects (higher CRT means, possible CRT overuse), and note MTurk may not be ideal for such studies (fn. 18, p. 1076).

One-shot manipulations embedded in attitude surveys do not replicate the repeated, cacophonous political information environment; the paper speaks to short-term cue-following on newly politicized issues, not stable attitudes (p. 1076).
Issues were chosen to be not yet strongly partisan, which limits generalization to already polarized issues (p. 1073).
Two ancillary studies lack a no-cues condition and cannot speak to presence vs absence of cues; the Danish study uses ideological rather than partisan identity (fn. 15).

The paper's explanation of issue-dependence (in-party vs out-party strength) is post hoc and speculative; sampling, method, and political environment differences across studies are not ruled out (p. 1074).
Speculation that elite polarization could be self-reinforcing through identity-driven conformity among reflective partisans is not tested here (p. 1076).
Panels are online, non-probability samples; representativeness is not reported in the main text. Study 2 N in text (1,302) differs from Table 3 (1,258).
measures: Partisan social identity strength: 8-item scale (Bankert, Huddy and Rosema 2017), averaged and rescaled 0-1; example item 'When I speak about the [party] I usually say we instead of they'. Asked of those identifying with or leaning to a party (pp. 1063-1064).

Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT): 3 items in study 1; 7 items (Toplak, West and Stanovich 2014) in studies 2 and 3; 7-item scale combining CRT-2 (4 items) and 3 CRT-7 items in study 4. Scored as proportion correct (pp. 1064-1065).
Need for cognition (NfC): 18-item scale (Cacioppo, Petty and Kao 1984) in studies 1 and 2; 10-item scale (Bakker and Lelkes 2018) in study 3; 0-1 rescaled. Not measured in study 4 (p. 1065).
Political knowledge: 10 multiple-choice items (ANES-style; Clifford and Jerit 2016) in study 2 only, proportion correct (p. 1065).
Latent cognitive resources: factor scores from a confirmatory factor analysis of all CRT, NfC and (study 2) knowledge items, rescaled 0-1; studies 1-3 (p. 1065).
Depth of processing (studies 3 and 4): reading time for the policy description; word count of thoughts listed after reading; factual quiz (four items food irradiation, two items farm) (p. 1068-1069).
Policy support: food irradiation on a 0-1 scale; farm subsidy on a seven-point item rescaled 0-1 (study 2, M = .71, SD = .25) (pp. 1063, 1066).
Covariates: gender, age (years), education (three levels), race (white vs nonwhite), party (Democrat vs Republican) (p. 1064).

summary_md:
Bakker, Lelkes and Malka ran four US survey experiments, plus two ancillary ones and a pooled individual-data meta-analysis, on partisans in online panels from 2016 to 2018. The issues (food irradiation and farm subsidies) were chosen because they were not yet partisan. The paper tests two accounts of why people follow party cues. Bounded rationality says low-resource citizens use cues to save effort. Expressive utility says strong identifiers with high cognitive resources use cues to protect their party identity.

Bounded rationality gets no support. Cue effects are no larger among low-CRT, low-NfC or low-knowledge respondents, and most interaction signs run the other way. Expressive utility gets partial support. In the meta-analysis, among high-resource respondents the in-party cue effect rises with partisan identity strength (slope .15 for NfC and latent resources), about 15 points from the weakest to the strongest identifiers. Only two of six three-way terms are significant, and the MTurk replication shows nothing.

The finding that matters most for Melange is the main-effect asymmetry. The out-party cue reduces support by .06 to .07 on a 0-1 scale, which is a significant repulsion. The in-party cue adds only about +.03 and is non-significant in studies 1 and 2. The engine cites this paper (paired with Furnas) for `cpf_pressure`, which scores co-partisan pressure at x1.7 and out-partisan pressure at a positive x0.5. The paper shows something different: out-party cues push the receiver away, and in-party cues are weak.

The subjects are members of the public reading one-shot survey vignettes, not legislators pressing other legislators. The evidence is therefore a direction-of-sign check for the engine, not a source for its constants.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues lower policy support: -0.06 (study 1, p<.01, N=747), -0.07 (study 2), and -0.07 in the pooled meta-analysis of studies 1-4. In-party cues add +0.03, non-significant in studies 1 and 2 and +0.03 pooled. The out-party effect is negative and larger in magnitude than the in-party effect, so no positive co-/out-partisan persuasion ratio exists to calibrate. The component's question, whether the ratio is near 1.7/0.5 = 3.4, is answered no: the out-party sign is reversed.

bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure returns 1.7 for co-partisans, 0.5 for out-partisans and 1.0 otherwise. The docstring labels this 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment'. flip_model sums PRO neighbours into nA and ANTI neighbours into nB, both weighted by cpf_pressure, so an out-party pro-CU neighbour still adds positive pull at half weight. The dashboard align() mirrors this with K.SRCPRO/K.SRCANTI.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The sign result transfers only as a direction check. The paper measures mass-public respondents' 0-1 support for low-salience policies after one cue embedded in a survey, from 2016 to 2018 online non-probability panels. It does not measure legislator-to-legislator pressure, cosponsorship, or repeated lobbying. Two numbers do not transfer: the 1.7 amplification (the paper's in-party effect is small and often null) and any positive out-party weight (the paper finds repulsion). Elite-level cue evidence, such as Box-Steffensmeier et al. on Dear Colleague letters, would be needed to set legislator-side constants.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues repel: about -0.07 on a 0-1 scale, pooled across studies 1-4. That is backfire, not a null. Heterogeneity in cue-following runs through partisan identity strength combined with cognitive resources (NfC, latent resources), not through any bipartisan-bridge attribute. The authors also note that real messages usually carry both in-party and out-party cues (p.1074).

Two parts of the design have no support in the paper: the bridge exemption (sqrt(bpf) restoring full positive cross-party influence) and the bpf gate itself, because the paper never measures bipartisanship. The scope is mass public on new issues, so even the sign is an analogy for elite cosponsorship recruitment.

extraction.title: Matching theory and Senate committee assignment
extraction.venue: Political Science Research and Methods, 1-25 (Original Article; open access)
extraction.document_type: Journal article (original research article; formal theory with descriptive and structural empirics)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,916 lines of the extracted file (main text pp. 1-20, references pp. 21-22, appendix Tables A1-A8 and Figure A1 pp. 23-25). Metadata hint confirmed (title, author, 2025, venue, DOI all match the text). Paul's markup: none (no markup files were supplied, so paul_markup is empty). Some appendix tables (A6, A7, A8, Table 1 layout) are garbled in the text extraction; numbers cited below are only those readable without ambiguity.
extraction.research_question: How do the US Senate parties actually assign members to committees, i.e., what matching mechanism does each party use to turn rank-ordered committee requests into assignments, and what do those mechanisms imply for strategic reporting, party discipline by the committee-on-committees (COC), incumbents' property rights, and the validity of canonical theories of legislative organization (Distributive, Informational, Cartel-Agenda)? (Sec. 1, pp. 2-3.)
extraction.theory: Matching theory (school-choice and house-allocation mechanisms: Serial Dictatorship, Boston mechanism, Top Trading Cycles / YRMH-IGYT, with existing-tenant and property-rights norms). Argues Senate Republicans use a strategyproof seniority-based Serial Dictatorship (equivalent to TTC/YRMH-IGYT in practice) and Senate Democrats use an approximation of the non-strategyproof Boston mechanism with COC tie-breaking. Revisits Distributive (Shepsle-Weingast), Informational (Gilligan-Krehbiel, Krehbiel) and Cartel-Agenda (Cox-McCubbins) theories (Sec. 2 and 4, pp. 3-5 and 16-18). Motivational theories (Mayhew reelection, Fenno power and policy, Ferejohn pork and monetary gain) are background (Sec. 2, p. 4).
extraction.data: Three sources. (1) Frisch and Kelly (2006) Senate Democrat committee request data, 80th-103rd Congresses (1947-1995); unit is a Democratic senator's ranked request. (2) Stewart and Woon (2005) Senate committee assignments, 103rd-114th Congresses (1993-2017); unit is a senator-committee assignment. (3) Novel archival dataset of Senate Republican committee requests from the Robert and Elizabeth Dole Archive (University of Kansas) for the 91st and 103rd Congresses (approx. 1969-1971 and 1993-1995); the paper does not report the number of Republican request records. Table A5 uses 104th-114th assignments with per-committee Ns (e.g., Small Business R=31, D=18; Environment R=30, D=14; Rules R=18, D=15). The structural section (Sec. 5.3) uses 426 new Senate committee assignments across 11 sessions (104th-114th), 25 committees and 97 distinct senators; each committee has 7-36 new assignments (fn. 22, p. 20). Ns for Figure 1 and Figure A1 are not reported. Figure A1 notes 76% of Republican non-freshmen rank only one choice, so only first choices are compared.
extraction.method: Primarily theoretical and descriptive. (a) Institutional reconstruction of the two procedures from CRS reports (Schneider 2003, 2006, 2014) and Shepsle (1978), with archival correspondence exhibits (Tables 1-2). (b) Mechanism-design analysis: static properties of SD, SD with squatting rights, SD with waiting list, TTC/YRMH-IGYT, and the Boston mechanism (Table 3, citing Abdulkadiroglu-Sonmez 1999, 2003; Kojima-Unver 2014). (c) A two-committee partial-equilibrium model of a single Democrat's rank-order choice against a stochastic environment with an existing-tenant guarantee u(x)>0, yielding Proposition 1 (higher guaranteed payoff implies weakly higher rank positions, p. 15; proof in Online Appendix A.2). (d) Descriptive comparisons: share of rank-1 requests by committee type, freshman vs non-freshman Democrats (Figure 1, p-values); Republican freshman vs non-freshman (Figure A1); average chamber seniority at request (Table A4); cross-party difference in means of seniority at appointment with t-stats and difference in SDs (Table A5); revealed-preference ranking of committee value using average seniority with the 1-3 most senior members excluded (Table A6). (e) Reduced-form structural model u_ic = delta_c + eps_i with eps_i mean 0 and variance sigma_eps^2, identifying committee common value and idiosyncratic variance from the mean and variance of chamber seniority at appointment (and minimum-seniority moments mu_min, sigma_min) for Republicans only (Tables A7-A8), justified by the seniority-based TTC/YRMH-IGYT mechanism. Cross-party comparisons assume the true preference distributions of Republicans and Democrats are the same (p. 19).
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. The paper calls its evidence "suggestive" (Sec. 5.1, p. 18). Identification of strategic behavior rests on mechanism-design logic: Republicans' SD/TTC mechanism is strategyproof, so reported requests are treated as true preferences (revealed preference), while Democrats' Boston mechanism is not, so requests are treated as strategic and predicted to vary by incumbency. Freshman vs non-freshman contrasts are the within-party comparison (Prediction 3a). Cross-party contrasts of seniority at appointment (Predictions 2b, 2c) are used to infer non-seniority tie-breaking or party discipline by the Democratic COC, under the stated assumption of equal true-preference distributions. Structural estimates of delta_c and sigma_eps are identified only if seniority at appointment reflects the TTC/YRMH-IGYT allocation and the additive utility form holds. Prediction 4 (committee value from seniority, excluding high-seniority members to net out queuing benefits) is argued by revealed preference.
extraction.scope: Population: US Senate party committee assignments (Republican and Democratic caucuses). Institution: Senate standing committees, categorized as Constituency, Policy, Prestige and Admin committees (Table A3) and as A/B/C committees (Table A1). Era: Democrat requests 1947-1995; Republican archival requests 91st and 103rd Congresses; assignments 1993-2017 (103rd-114th), with the structural analysis on 104th-114th. Excludes the House as a test case (discussed as background), and post-election seat-ratio negotiations (fn. 9).

key_findings.finding: Senate Republicans assign committees via a seniority-based Serial Dictatorship approximated in practice by the TTC/YRMH-IGYT mechanism; it is strategyproof, individually rational and Pareto efficient. Senate Democrats use an approximation of the Boston mechanism with COC tie-breaking votes, which is not strategyproof. The two parties therefore use structurally different mechanisms.
key_findings.location: Abstract p. 1; Introduction pp. 2-3; Sec. 3.1-3.3 pp. 7-9; Table 3 p. 14; Sec. 3.5.1 pp. 12-14
key_findings.numbers: Table 3: Democrat Boston mechanism is not strategyproof; Republican SD with seniority is strategyproof but not IR; SD with squatting rights is strategyproof but neither IR nor PE; SD with waiting list is strategyproof and IR but not PE; TTC/YRMH-IGYT is strategyproof, IR and PE.

key_findings.finding: Prediction 1 (Republicans request truthfully, Democrats strategically) is supported only by archival anecdote and a CRS quote; the paper says it lacks enough data to test Prediction 1 directly.

No systematic Senate Republican request dataset exists for testing Prediction 1, 2(a) or 3(b) (p. 18). Republican request data are archival, limited to the 91st and 103rd Congresses, and the number of records is not reported.
Cross-party comparisons assume the distribution of true preferences is identical for Republicans and Democrats (p. 19); relaxing this would need matching or structural estimation, which was not done.
Only first-choice requests are compared for Republicans, because 76% of non-freshman Republicans rank one choice (Figure A1 note, p. 25).
The freshman vs non-freshman Democratic difference (8%, p = 0.15) is not significant at conventional levels.

Republican strategyproofness is supported partly by archival anecdote (Exhibit #4) and the Dole letter (Exhibit #5); Exhibit #6 (sequential implementation) is also anecdotal.
Interdependent preferences (over who else sits on a committee, or House counterparts) would break strategyproofness of both mechanisms (fn. 13, p. 9).
The author treats seniority-only tie-breaking as unlikely for Democrats (p. 18), but rival tie-breaking criteria are not formally tested.
Queuing benefits and specialization stickiness confound interpreting high seniority on a committee as revealed value (p. 16).
Party discipline is modeled only through Democratic COC tie-breaking; Republican leader influence is shown only through the Dole exhibits (Sec. 3.4, pp. 10-11).
The Republican mechanism is a static SD/TTC approximation; dynamic rules and sequential implementation are simplified (fn. 7 p. 6; fn. 17 p. 14).

short_quotes.quote: Republicans and Democrats use two distinct matching mechanisms, such that canonical theories of parties cannot apply equally to them.
The Republican mechanism is strategyproof, whereas the Democrat mechanism incentivizes politicians to manipulate their reported preferences.

summary_md:
Thakur (PSRM 2025) applies matching theory to US Senate committee assignment. He argues that the two parties fill seats through different mechanisms. Senate Republicans use a seniority-ordered Serial Dictatorship, which works in practice like the strategyproof, individually rational and Pareto-efficient TTC/YRMH-IGYT. Senate Democrats use something close to the Boston mechanism, with secret tie-breaking votes by the committee-on-committees (COC). Under the Boston mechanism, members have reason to misreport their preferences.

The evidence is explicitly suggestive.
- Freshman Democrats list Prestige committees as first choice 8% less often than non-freshmen (p = 0.15, 1947-1995 request data). Republicans show no such gap (p = 0.80).
- Mean seniority at appointment differs across parties on some committees (e.g., Environment & Public Works: R 3.80, N=30, vs D 1.00, N=14; t=3.05). The author reads this as possible COC discipline on the Democratic side.
- A reduced-form structural model for Republicans only (426 new assignments, 104th-114th) finds high common value and small idiosyncratic variance for Finance and Appropriations. Constituency committees such as Small Business have low common value and depend on constituency particulars.
- Seniority on a committee mixes revealed value with queuing benefits.

For Paul's system, the paper speaks mainly to the committee/Influence pillar. That pillar prices seats by CU-relevance tier, with fixed chair and ranking multipliers. It does not distinguish chamber or party. The paper suggests that who holds a seat is partly an artifact of party-specific mechanisms, seniority queues and COC discipline. This bears on Paul's chicken-or-egg note about partisanship and committee selection. It also argues against treating committee office as a costly, member-chosen signal, which agrees with the system dropping committee gatekeeping (path J) from the say-do gate.

Scope limits: Senate only (about 100 of 533 members), data from 1947-2017, the House not studied, and no causal identification. None of this validates the tier weights. Any test of the committee pillar against outcomes should be stratified by party and chamber, or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Senate seat allocation runs through two different party mechanisms. Republicans use seniority-ordered SD/TTC (strategyproof). Democrats use a Boston approximation with secret COC tie-breaking. Cross-party seniority-at-appointment gaps on some committees point to party discipline: Environment & Public Works R 3.80 (N=30) vs D 1.00 (N=14), diff 2.80, t=3.05; Commerce diff -1.74, t=-2.09; 104th-114th assignments. So who holds a given seat reflects mechanism, seniority queue and party selection, not only member choice or structural power.
bearings.system_side: Influence% = committee_raw/MAX, built from seat tokens priced by CU-relevance tier (Highly 3.0 / Moderately 1.8 / Slightly 0.9; subcommittee 1/6) with chair, ranking and vice multipliers. The same rule applies to every member regardless of chamber or party, and the result is weighted at 40% of the composite. The pillar treats a held seat as structural CU power.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Covers only the Senate rows (about 100 of 533). The paper does not study the House or the 119th-Congress rules, and its evidence is suggestive (p. 18). The bearing does not challenge the CU-relevance tiers, which are owner policy. It says that any test of whether committee score predicts CU outcomes should be stratified by party and chamber, or labelled UNSTRATIFIED, because selection into seats differs by party. Moderate at most, since the cross-party gaps are significant on only a few committees.

Rules, Finance, Governmental Affairs and Appropriations are the most sought after even after excluding the 1-3 most senior members. High within-committee seniority mixes value with queuing benefits.

gaps_exposed: The committee pillar is the same for both chambers and both parties. Nothing records how the seat was obtained (seniority queue vs COC selection) or the member's seniority. The paper shows that selection into seats differs by party, so committee-score validity is untested within strata.

There is no committee-value (prestige or common-value) term separate from CU relevance. A Highly seat on a low-common-value constituency committee such as Small Business and a Highly seat on a high-value policy committee are priced identically.
Chair and ranking multipliers ignore that Senate leadership largely follows within-committee seniority queues. The paper flags queuing benefits as confounding seniority read as value.
flags: The pillar effectively pools across a fault line the paper identifies: the Republican seniority mechanism vs Democratic COC tie-breaking. Any committee-score coefficient or correlation against outcomes must be reported by party (and chamber), or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

The paper's evidence is self-described as suggestive. Key contrasts are not significant at conventional levels (Democrat freshman gap p=0.15), and Table A6-A8 numbers are garbled in extraction. Do not quote committee value estimates from it.
Senate only (about 100 of 533 members). Nothing transfers to House seat-holders without separate evidence.
This mapping is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Hall & Wayman (1990) and Fouirnaies & Hall (2018), cited here on lobbying and committee access, are background only. Neither licenses access or influence language for committee seats in the system.
paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's committee-pillar note flagging a chicken-or-egg problem between partisanship and committee selection. It gives a mechanism for that worry: Democratic COC tie-breaking can discipline placement, while Republican placement is mostly seniority. The paper does not support Paul's broader premise that committees are the structural power layer (Porter) in any way that would underwrite the tier weights or the 40% Influence weight. Those weights remain owner policy that this paper does not test. Paul's note is not stale; the system has since removed committee gatekeeping from the say-do gate, which fits this paper. The note does not yet record that seat selection differs by party, which matters for any future validation of the committee pillar.

related.why: Porter maps House committee structure as networks of shared membership. Thakur explains how Senate seats are allocated, which bears on whether shared-membership ties reflect choice or party mechanism.
A House committee-request codebook is the same kind of request data as Thakur's Frisch-Kelly and Dole archive requests. It could support a House version of his freshman vs incumbent request tests.

Paul cites Huneeus & Kim's committee-assignment instrument. Thakur's finding that placement follows party-specific mechanisms (seniority vs COC discipline) bears on how exogenous assignment is as an instrument.
Paul reads Gaynor as showing that party leadership shapes members' insulation. Thakur models leader and COC discipline over committee placement, a parallel party-control channel.

extraction.research_question: Can an improved D* Lite incremental search, combined with map zooming and path smoothing, plan safe, short, real-time 3D paths for firefighting UAVs that reach suspected fire spots and UGVs (refuelling/material stations) when the 3D workspace is partly or wholly unknown?
extraction.theory: No social or economic theory. The framing is algorithmic: D* Lite incremental/heuristic search (Koenig-style, cited as [4], [5]), a hierarchical/partitioned A* idea (HPA*, described in Sec. II intro, not referenced), and Catmull-Rom spline smoothing ([8]).
extraction.data: Simulated 3D grid environments only, with no real forest data. Table 1: six environments (Env1-2 120x120x100 m; Env3-6 100x100x100 m), obstacle densities 0%, 1%, 5%, cuboid obstacles plus random 5x5x5 m^3 obstacles; single static target. Table 2: four improved-only environments (Env1-2 100x100x100 m; Env3-4 120x120x100 m). Fig. 6: four environments with multiple static targets. Fig. 7: one scenario with a dynamic target (UGV). Unit = one simulated planning run per scenario; no run count or repetitions reported. No time period (2020 paper). Hardware: Intel Core i7-9700, Ubuntu 18.04, Python 2.
extraction.method: Improved D* Lite (Sec. II.B, steps 1-7, p.4234-4235): (1) zoom the map out to a quarter of its size; (2) if Euclidean start-to-goal distance is below 28, run plain D* Lite, otherwise plan on the shrunken map with reverse search from the target; (3) scan obstacles with radar range r = 20 m and refine a local window d = 2r = 40 m; (4) smooth the path with two methods: sight-line node removal (method 1) and centripetal Catmull-Rom spline insertion (method 2); (5) fill the trajectory where node coordinates differ by more than 1 on any axis; (6) re-plan when the path is invalidated (next node more than r away, or target moved). Heuristic h is the maximum absolute coordinate difference (Chebyshev-type). Multiple targets are visited greedily by nearest remaining Euclidean distance (Eq. 3, Sec. III.B). The UAV is treated as a point particle with dynamics neglected (Sec. III, p.4235).
extraction.scope: Population: simulated forest firefighting UAVs (plus UGVs as moving targets), not real flights. Institution: Xi'an University of Technology and Concordia University. Era: 2020. Results are for synthetic grids with one static target per run in Table 1, and UGV tracking in one dynamic scenario.
